---
title: "Non-deterministic finite-state automata"
bibliography: ../../formal_complexity.bib
---

A *non-deterministic* finite-state automaton loosens some of the restrictions imposed by a DFA;
chiefly, by allowing the transitions between states to be characterized by a *relation*, rather than by a function.
@partee_mathematical_1990, Definition 17.6 (p. 462), presents them as follows.

As non-deterministic finite-state automaton (NFA) is a quintuple $⟨K, Σ, Δ, q_{0}, F⟩$, where:

- $K$ is a finite set, the set of *states*.
- $Σ$ is a finite set, the *alphabet*.
- $q_{0}$ is a special element of $K$ (i.e., $q_{0} ∈ K$), called the *initial state*.
- $F$ is a special subset of $K$ (i.e., $F ⊆ K$) whose elements are *final states*.
- $Δ$ is a relation on $K × Σ^{*}$ and $K$ (i.e., $Δ ⊆ (K × Σ^{*}) × K$), called the *transition relation*.

Instead of a function $δ$, we have a relation $Δ$ which associates pairs of states from $K$ and strings over the alphabet with new states from $K$.
It is because $Δ$ can associate any given pair of input state and string with potentially more than one output state that we say NFAs are *non-deterministic*.

Note also that this definition of NFAs allows not only words---but *strings*---to be associated with the transition from one state to the next.

## Example

For illustration, consider a finite language over the alphabet $\{a, b, c\}$;
say, the language $\{ac, abc, bc\}$.
We can characterize this language using the following NFA.

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 3
//| fig-height: 1.4

digraph NFA {
  rankdir=LR;

  graph [
    margin=0,
    pad=0,
    splines=true,
    nodesep=0.45,
    ranksep=0.45
  ];

  node [
    shape=circle,
    width=0.4,
    height=0.4,
    fontsize=10
  ];

  edge [
    fontsize=10,
    arrowsize=0.25
  ];

  start [
    shape=none,
    label="",
    width=0,
    height=0,
    margin=0
  ];

  q0 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB>0</SUB>>];
  q1 [label=<<I>q</I><SUB>1</SUB>>, shape=doublecircle];

  start:e -> q0:w;

  q0 -> q1 [label=<<I>ac</I>>];
  q0 -> q1 [label=<<I>abc</I>>];
  q0 -> q1 [label=<<I>bc</I>>];
}
```

- $K = \{q_{0}, q_{1}\}$
- $Σ = \{a, b, c\}$
- $F = \{q_{1}\}$
- $Δ = \{⟨q_{0}, s, q_{1}⟩ ∣ s ∈ \{ac, abc, bc\}\}$

More generally, given any finite language $L = \{s_{1}, ..., s_{n}\}$ over some alphabet $Σ$, we can define the NFA which accepts exactly the strings in this language by using the above construction and defining
$$Δ = \{⟨q_{0}, s, q_{1}⟩ ∣ s ∈ L\}$$
